Coverage: building a 2D prefix table for $O(1)$ sub-rectangle sums; the 2D difference array that inverts it; the same inclusion–exclusion in three (and $d$) dimensions; adding an arithmetic progression to a range with a second-order difference; prefix sums taken along the two diagonal families of a grid; and weighted sums where each element contributes $\text{count}\times\text{value}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"}
- Answer the sum of any axis-aligned sub-rectangle of a static grid in $O(1)$ after one $O(nm)$ build, using the four-corner inclusion–exclusion (@sec-nd-a1, @sec-nd-p1-rectsum).
- Apply many **rectangle adds** in $O(1)$ each by writing to four corners of a **2D difference array** and running a single prefix to recover the values (@sec-nd-a2, @sec-nd-p2-rectadd).
- Generalise the prefix to 3D and to $d$ dimensions, knowing the query touches $2^d$ corners with alternating signs (@sec-nd-a3, @sec-nd-p2-3dbox).
- Add an **arithmetic progression** (a linear function of the index) to a range in $O(1)$ with a second-order difference array, and materialise the result with two scans (@sec-nd-a4, @sec-nd-p3-aprange).

- Recognise a **weighted / contribution** sum — "each element is counted a known number of times" — and turn it into one prefix-style pass, as in counting $g(x)=k$ over a range or a digit-position weight (@sec-nd-a6, @sec-nd-p1-rq, @sec-nd-p4-rybinsk).
- Triage a statement into 1D prefix, 2D / $d$-dim prefix, difference array, Fenwick/2D-BIT (dynamic), or Mo/sqrt (offline) — and spot the matrix-tagged problems that are really DP or segment trees (@sec-nd-a6).
:::

## Why this matters {#sec-nd-why}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A **prefix sum** turns "add up this slice" into "subtract two precomputed numbers." Chapter @sec-pref did it on a line: build $P[i] = a_0 + \dots + a_{i-1}$ once, then $\sum_{i=l}^{r} a_i = P[r+1] - P[l]$ in $O(1)$. This chapter asks what happens when the data is not a line. Paint the values on a grid and the same idea survives with one more term: build a table $P$ of running sums and read any **sub-rectangle** off its four corners. Run the trick in reverse and you get the **difference array** — instead of answering sums you *make* changes, and a whole batch of rectangle-adds collapses to four corner writes each. The machinery stretches cleanly to three dimensions and beyond ($2^d$ corners), and it bends to cover subtler shapes — diagonals of a grid, or an arithmetic progression sprinkled onto a range.
:::

Chapter @sec-pref gave you the 1D prefix sum and its inverse, the difference array. Those two tools answer an enormous fraction of "sum over a range" questions, but they assume the array is a **line** and the updates are **constant additions**. Real problems break both assumptions: images, game boards, spreadsheet ranges, and "sum over this box of the cube" all live in two or three dimensions, and "add $1,2,3,\dots$ to this range" or "add $5$ to every cell of this rectangle" are linear *changes*, not point updates. Every one of those is still a prefix sum — you just need the right shape of table and the right number of corners.

The unifying move across the whole chapter is **inclusion–exclusion over precomputed partial sums**. Once you see that a 2D prefix query is "big block, minus two edges, plus the corner you subtracted twice," the 3D version (eight corners), the diagonal version, and the weighted/multiplicity version all fall out of the same picture. The decision of *which* table to build is the skill this chapter trains:

| Statement hint | What it really is | Which section solves it |
|---|---|---|
| "static grid, many *sum of this rectangle* questions" | 2D prefix table, $O(1)$ per query | @sec-nd-a1, @sec-nd-p1 |
| "apply many *add $v$ to this whole rectangle*, then read the grid" | 2D difference array (inverse of the prefix) | @sec-nd-a2, @sec-nd-p2 |
| "3D array / cube, sum over a box" | $d$-dimensional prefix, $2^d$ corners | @sec-nd-a3, @sec-nd-p2 |
| "add an arithmetic progression (or $a\cdot i+b$) to $[\ell,r]$, many times" | second-order difference; two final scans | @sec-nd-a4, @sec-nd-p3 |
| "sum a run of cells along a diagonal; or count $x\in[\ell,r]$ with property $p$" | diagonal prefix families / value-domain prefix | @sec-nd-a5, @sec-nd-p1, @sec-nd-p4 |
| "each element is counted a known number of times, or weighted by its position" | weighted / contribution sum | @sec-nd-a6, @sec-nd-p4 |

One table, two directions. Read it forward (cumulate the cells into a table of partial sums) to *answer* many range/box/diagonal sums in $O(1)$; read it backward (record changes in a difference array) to *apply* many range/rectangle changes in $O(1)$ each, then recover the values with a single scan.

:::

The lessons build the toolkit in six steps, then Part B turns each into a solved pattern:

- **A1 — The 2D prefix sum.** Build $P$ once; any sub-rectangle is four corners (@sec-nd-a1).
- **A2 — The 2D difference array.** Rectangle adds in $O(1)$; the exact inverse of A1 (@sec-nd-a2).
- **A3 — Higher dimensions.** 3D prefix and the $2^d$-corner rule (@sec-nd-a3).
- **A4 — Progressions on ranges.** A second-order difference adds a linear function to a range in $O(1)$ (@sec-nd-a4).
- **A5 — Diagonal prefix sums.** Precompute along $i-j$ and $i+j$ for $O(1)$ diagonal runs (@sec-nd-a5).
- **A6 — Weighted sums & triage.** Multiplicity/contribution sums, and choosing prefix vs difference vs BIT vs Mo (@sec-nd-a6).

Part B runs four patterns: prefix sums in one and two dimensions (@sec-nd-p1), the 2D difference array and higher dimensions (@sec-nd-p2), higher-order differences for progressions on ranges (@sec-nd-p3), and diagonal & weighted prefix sums (@sec-nd-p4).

## Part A — Lessons

## A1. The 2D prefix sum {#sec-nd-a1}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Lay the numbers out in an $n\times m$ grid. Build a table $P$ of size $(n{+}1)\times(m{+}1)$ where $P[i][j]$ is the sum of the rectangle from the top-left corner down to (but not including) row $i$, column $j$ — that is, all cells $(r,c)$ with $r < i$ and $c < j$. You fill it one cell at a time with $P[i{+}1][j{+}1] = P[i][j{+}1] + P[i{+}1][j] - P[i][j] + a[i][j]$: add the row above, add the column to the left, subtract the top-left overlap you counted twice, then drop in the current cell. Now the sum of *any* sub-rectangle with corners $(r_0,c_0)$ (inclusive) and $(r_1,c_1)$ (exclusive) is $P[r_1][c_1] - P[r_0][c_1] - P[r_1][c_0] + P[r_0][c_0]$. Take the big top-left block, remove the strip above and the strip to the left, and put back the corner you removed twice. Build in $O(nm)$, answer in $O(1)$.
:::

Here is the whole engine. Read the `rowsum` line as "everything to the left in this row, plus the block above" — that is $P[i][j{+}1] + \text{rowsum}$, the same recurrence in a form that avoids a temporary:

```{python}
def build_prefix2d(a):
    """a: n rows of m ints. Return P of size (n+1)x(m+1) with P[i][j] the sum of the
    rectangle of cells (r, c), r < i and c < j. Row 0 and column 0 are all zero."""
    n = len(a)
    m = len(a[0]) if n else 0
    P = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(n):
        rowsum = 0
        for j in range(m):
            rowsum += a[i][j]                 # a[i][0] + ... + a[i][j]
            P[i + 1][j + 1] = P[i][j + 1] + rowsum
    return P


def rect_sum(P, r0, c0, r1, c1):
    """Sum of cells (r, c) with r0 <= r < r1 and c0 <= c < c1. 0-indexed, half-open."""
    return P[r1][c1] - P[r0][c1] - P[r1][c0] + P[r0][c0]


def rect_sum_brute(a, r0, c0, r1, c1):
    return sum(a[i][j] for i in range(r0, r1) for j in range(c0, c1))


a = [[1, 2, 3],
     [4, 5, 6],
     [7, 8, 9]]
P = build_prefix2d(a)
assert P[3][3] == 45                              # whole grid
assert rect_sum(P, 1, 1, 3, 3) == 5 + 6 + 8 + 9   # bottom-right 2x2
assert rect_sum(P, 0, 0, 1, 3) == 1 + 2 + 3       # top row
```

The recurrence is the whole idea; here it is checked against the $O(\text{area})$ brute force on hundreds of random grids and rectangles, exactly as Chapter @sec-pref stress-checked the 1D version:

```{python}
for _ in range(400):
    n = random.randint(1, 8)
    m = random.randint(1, 8)
    a = [[random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(n)]
    P = build_prefix2d(a)
    r0 = random.randrange(n); r1 = random.randrange(r0 + 1, n + 1)
    c0 = random.randrange(m); c1 = random.randrange(c0 + 1, m + 1)
    assert rect_sum(P, r0, c0, r1, c1) == rect_sum_brute(a, r0, c0, r1, c1)
```

gp = build_prefix2d(ga)
cells = [[str(gp[i][j]) for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)]
# colour the four query corners of rect_sum(P, 1, 1, 3, 3): +P[3][3], -P[1][3], -P[3][1], +P[1][1]
colors = {(3, 3): "green", (1, 3): "pink", (3, 1): "pink", (1, 1): "indigo"}

The prefix table $P$ of $[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]$. To sum the bottom-right $2\times2$ block, read the green corner $P[3][3]=45$, subtract the two pink corners, and add back the indigo overlap: $45 - 6 - 12 + 1 = 28$.

:::

**Overflow, now.** A grid of $n\cdot m$ cells each up to $10^{9}$ has a total sum up to $10^{15}$ — comfortably past 32-bit. Keep $P$ and every corner expression in a 64-bit integer (`long long`). This is the first place a 1D habit of using `int` bites, and it recurs harder in @sec-nd-a6.

## A2. The 2D difference array {#sec-nd-a2}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
The prefix sum *answers* range questions; the **difference array** *makes* range changes, and it is the prefix run backwards. On a line (@sec-pref) you add $v$ to every cell of $[\ell, r)$ by writing $D[\ell] \mathrel{+}= v$, $D[r] \mathrel{-}= v$ and taking one prefix sum at the end. On a grid the same idea opens a rectangle with **four** corner writes: to add $v$ to all cells $r_0 \le r < r_1$, $c_0 \le c < c_1$, set $D[r_0][c_0] \mathrel{+}= v$, $D[r_1][c_0] \mathrel{-}= v$, $D[r_0][c_1] \mathrel{-}= v$, $D[r_1][c_1] \mathrel{+}= v$. Do all your rectangle adds in $O(1)$ each, then run a single 2D prefix over $D$ and the actual grid values appear. Because a prefix undoes a difference, you already own both directions of the tool.
:::

Allocate $D$ one row and one column larger than the grid so the $r_1$ and $c_1$ boundary writes always land in range. Recovering the values is literally `build_prefix2d` from A1 applied to $D$:

```{python}
def apply_rect_diff(D, r0, c0, r1, c1, v):
    """Add v to every cell (r, c) with r0 <= r < r1 and c0 <= c < c1.
    D must be at least (r1+1) x (c1+1); O(1) per call."""
    D[r0][c0] += v
    D[r1][c0] -= v
    D[r0][c1] -= v
    D[r1][c1] += v


def recover2d(D, n, m):
    """The n x m value grid after all rectangle adds: a 2D prefix of the difference array."""
    P = build_prefix2d(D)                 # D is (n+1) x (m+1); P is (n+2) x (m+2)
    return [[P[i + 1][j + 1] for j in range(m)] for i in range(n)]


def rectadd_brute(n, m, ops):
    a = [[0] * m for _ in range(n)]
    for (r0, c0, r1, c1, v) in ops:
        for i in range(r0, r1):
            for j in range(c0, c1):
                a[i][j] += v
    return a


# one add of 5 to the middle 2x2 of a 4x4 grid
D = [[0] * 5 for _ in range(5)]
apply_rect_diff(D, 1, 1, 3, 3, 5)
got = recover2d(D, 4, 4)
assert got == rectadd_brute(4, 4, [(1, 1, 3, 3, 5)])
assert got[0][0] == 0 and got[1][1] == 5 and got[2][2] == 5 and got[3][3] == 0
```

```{python}
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 7); m = random.randint(1, 7)
    ops = []
    for _ in range(random.randint(0, 8)):
        r0 = random.randrange(n); r1 = random.randrange(r0 + 1, n + 1)
        c0 = random.randrange(m); c1 = random.randrange(c0 + 1, m + 1)
        ops.append((r0, c0, r1, c1, random.randint(-5, 5)))
    D = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for op in ops:
        apply_rect_diff(D, *op)
    assert recover2d(D, n, m) == rectadd_brute(n, m, ops)
```

The difference array $D$ after one rectangle add $v=5$ to $[r_0, r_1)\times[c_0, c_1)$: only four cells change (the two $+$ corners green, the two $-$ corners pink). A single 2D prefix turns these four marks into a solid block of $5$s — that is A1 running in reverse.

:::

A2 and A1 are the same object seen twice: a grid *is* the difference array of its prefix, and a difference array *is* the prefix-inverse of a grid. Whenever a statement says "several range updates first, then read everything" the difference form wins on speed; whenever it says "read a range sum, many times" the prefix form wins. The next problem pair (@sec-nd-p2) makes that choice concrete.

## A3. Higher dimensions {#sec-nd-a3}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Nothing about the 2D trick is special to two axes. Fill a $d$-dimensional table so that each entry $P[\text{idx}]$ sums every cell weakly inside the box from the origin to idx; a query over that box is one signed term per corner, with sign $(-1)^{\text{number of lowered coordinates}}$. In 2D there are $2^2 = 4$ corners; in 3D there are $2^3 = 8$; generally a query or a cell update touches $2^d$ partial sums. The 3D build $P[i][j][k]$ follows the same "add the three faces, subtract the three edges, add the corner" inclusion–exclusion, and a box sum peels off the same eight terms. Grow $d$ and the bookkeeping doubles each dimension — so the technique is stated for 3D and the general rule, not pushed to exotic $d$.
:::

The eight-term 3D recurrence below is the 2D rowsum trick applied along the third axis. `box_sum` reuses the *same* inclusion–exclusion signs you just learned, one index lower on each coordinate:

```{python}
def build_prefix3d(a):
    """a: n x m x k. P[i+1][j+1][t+1] = sum over r<=i, c<=j, s<=t. 8-term inclusion-exclusion."""
    n = len(a); m = len(a[0]); k = len(a[0][0])
    P = [[[0] * (k + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(m):
            for t in range(k):
                P[i + 1][j + 1][t + 1] = (a[i][j][t]
                    + P[i][j + 1][t + 1] + P[i + 1][j][t + 1] + P[i + 1][j + 1][t]
                    - P[i][j][t + 1] - P[i][j + 1][t] - P[i + 1][j][t]
                    + P[i][j][t])
    return P


def box_sum(P, i0, j0, k0, i1, j1, k1):
    """Sum over [i0,i1) x [j0,j1) x [k0,k1). Eight corners, signs by parity of index lowered."""
    return (P[i1][j1][k1] - P[i0][j1][k1] - P[i1][j0][k1] - P[i1][j1][k0]
            + P[i0][j0][k1] + P[i0][j1][k0] + P[i1][j0][k0] - P[i0][j0][k0])


def box_sum_brute(a, i0, j0, k0, i1, j1, k1):
    return sum(a[i][j][t] for i in range(i0, i1) for j in range(j0, j1) for t in range(k0, k1))


for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 4); m = random.randint(1, 4); k = random.randint(1, 4)
    a = [[[random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(k)] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(n)]
    P = build_prefix3d(a)
    i0 = random.randrange(n); i1 = random.randrange(i0 + 1, n + 1)
    j0 = random.randrange(m); j1 = random.randrange(j0 + 1, m + 1)
    k0 = random.randrange(k); k1 = random.randrange(k0 + 1, k + 1)
    assert box_sum(P, i0, j0, k0, i1, j1, k1) == box_sum_brute(a, i0, j0, k0, i1, j1, k1)
```

A $2\times2\times2$ block: the far green corner is the full box, the three pink faces subtract the parts beyond each lower bound, the three indigo edges add back pairs, and the near violet corner subtracts the one counted thrice. Eight corners, alternating signs — the $2^3$ instance of the same picture as A1's four corners.

:::

The general rule to carry forward: a $d$-dimensional prefix query is a signed sum of $2^d$ stored partial sums, and a point update in the *difference* view writes $2^d$ corners. Everything else in this chapter is choosing the right axes (rows and columns in A1–A2, the index in A4, a diagonal coordinate in A5) to pour into that framework.

## A4. Arithmetic progressions on ranges {#sec-nd-a4}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A difference array handles adding a *constant* to a range in $O(1)$. What if the thing you add grows — an **arithmetic progression** $t, t+d, t+2d, \dots$ poured onto $[\ell, r]$? Look at the added value as a function of the position $i$: on the range it is $d\cdot i + (t - d\cdot \ell)$, a *linear function of the index*. A linear function becomes constant after **one** differencing, so keep two running difference arrays — one accumulating the coefficient of $i$, one the constant term — patch four boundary points per update in $O(1)$, and rebuild the array with two prefix scans at the end. Stated the other way, a second-order difference array (take the difference twice) turns "add a progression" into "add a constant." This is the $k$-th-order trick with $k=1$; a degree-$k$ polynomial range-add needs order $k{+}1$ and binomial weights, but the two-array linear form is what almost every contest problem actually asks for.
:::

Each update $(\ell, r, t, d)$ (0-indexed, inclusive) adds $t + (i-\ell)\,d$ to cell $i$; rewrite that as $(d)\cdot i + (t-\ell d)$ and split the coefficient and constant across two first-difference arrays:

```{python}
def ap_range_add_brute(n, ops):
    a = [0] * n
    for (l, r, t, d) in ops:
        cur = t
        for i in range(l, r + 1):
            a[i] += cur
            cur += d
    return a


def ap_range_add_fast(n, ops):
    """ops: (l, r, t, d) 0-indexed inclusive; add t, t+d, t+2d, ... to a[l], a[l+1], ...
    Each add(i) = d*i + (t - l*d): one diff array for the slope, one for the intercept."""
    B = [0] * (n + 1)   # coefficient of i
    C = [0] * (n + 1)   # constant term
    for (l, r, t, d) in ops:
        alpha = d
        beta = t - l * d
        B[l] += alpha; B[r + 1] -= alpha
        C[l] += beta;  C[r + 1] -= beta
    a = [0] * n
    cb = cc = 0
    for i in range(n):
        cb += B[i]; cc += C[i]
        a[i] = cb * i + cc
    return a


# add 3,5,7 to cells 1..3 of a length-6 array
assert ap_range_add_fast(6, [(1, 3, 3, 2)]) == [0, 3, 5, 7, 0, 0]
assert ap_range_add_fast(6, [(1, 3, 3, 2)]) == ap_range_add_brute(6, [(1, 3, 3, 2)])

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 12)
    ops = []
    for _ in range(random.randint(0, 6)):
        l = random.randrange(n); r = random.randrange(l, n)
        ops.append((l, r, random.randint(-4, 4), random.randint(-3, 3)))
    assert ap_range_add_fast(n, ops) == ap_range_add_brute(n, ops)
```

::: {#fig-nd-a4}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
prog = ap_range_add_fast(8, [(1, 5, 2, 3)])   # adds 2,5,8,11,14 to indices 1..5
def draw(ax, p):
    V.bars(ax, p, prog, x=0.0, y=0.0,
           colors={i: "indigo" for i in range(1, 6)})
    V.array(ax, p, prog, x=0.0, y=-4.6,
            regions=[(1, 6, "indigo", "AP added on $[1,5]$")])
V.show(draw)
```

The result of pouring one progression onto $[1,5]$: a straight ramp rises across exactly the updated cells. Two boundary writes to the slope array and two to the intercept array built the whole ramp; the two prefix scans on the right turned those four marks back into values.

:::

The cost is $O(1)$ per update and $O(n)$ to materialise once at the end — versus $O(\text{length})$ per update for the brute force. If the queries interleave *reads* of the running array with the AP adds, you no longer have the "all updates, then read" luxury; that dynamic mix is a Fenwick-tree question (@sec-ds), noted in the triage of A6.

## A5. Diagonal prefix sums {#sec-nd-a5}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Sometimes the "range" you must sum is not an axis-aligned rectangle but a **run of cells along a diagonal**. A grid has two diagonal families: the `\`-diagonals where $i - j$ is constant, and the `/`-diagonals where $i + j$ is constant. Number the cells of each diagonal in order and lay a plain 1D prefix sum along it — one list per diagonal, indexed by the family key ($i-j$, shifted non-negative, or $i+j$). Then any contiguous segment *within* one diagonal is a difference of two stored prefix entries, exactly the 1D trick of @sec-pref, just applied to a slanted slice of the array.
:::

Walk cells top-to-bottom so the order along each diagonal is well defined, bucket by the diagonal key, and run a 1D prefix inside every bucket:

```{python}
def build_diag_prefixes(a):
    """Return (main, anti, Pmain, Panti). main[d] lists cells with i-j=d in increasing i;
    anti[s] lists cells with i+j=s in increasing i. Pmain[d] / Panti[s] are the 1D prefix
    sums (with a leading 0) of the values along that diagonal."""
    n = len(a); m = len(a[0])
    main = defaultdict(list); anti = defaultdict(list)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(m):
            main[i - j].append((i, j, a[i][j]))
            anti[i + j].append((i, j, a[i][j]))
    Pmain = {}; Panti = {}
    for d, cells in main.items():
        ps = [0]
        for _, _, v in cells:
            ps.append(ps[-1] + v)
        Pmain[d] = ps
    for s, cells in anti.items():
        ps = [0]
        for _, _, v in cells:
            ps.append(ps[-1] + v)
        Panti[s] = ps
    return main, anti, Pmain, Panti


def diag_segment_sum(P, key, lo, hi):
    """Sum positions lo..hi (inclusive, in bucket order) along one diagonal."""
    return P[key][hi + 1] - P[key][lo]


ga = [[1, 2, 3],
      [4, 5, 6],
      [7, 8, 9]]
main, anti, Pmain, Panti = build_diag_prefixes(ga)
# the main diagonal i-j=0 is [1,5,9]; the whole thing sums to 15
assert diag_segment_sum(Pmain, 0, 0, 2) == 15
assert diag_segment_sum(Pmain, 0, 1, 2) == 5 + 9      # a contiguous sub-run

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 6); m = random.randint(1, 6)
    a = [[random.randint(-6, 6) for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(n)]
    main, anti, Pmain, Panti = build_diag_prefixes(a)
    d = random.choice(list(main.keys()))
    cells = main[d]
    lo = random.randrange(len(cells)); hi = random.randrange(lo, len(cells))
    assert diag_segment_sum(Pmain, d, lo, hi) == sum(cells[t][2] for t in range(lo, hi + 1))
```

::: {#fig-nd-a5}

col = {(0, 0): "green", (1, 1): "green", (2, 2): "green",     # i-j=0
       (0, 2): "indigo", (2, 0): "indigo"}                     # i+j=2 corner cells
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, cells, x=0.0, y=0.0,
           row_labels=["i=0", "i=1", "i=2"], col_labels=["j=0", "j=1", "j=2"],

The `\`-diagonal $i-j=0$ (green, values $1,5,9$) and two cells of a `/`-diagonal $i+j$ (indigo) of the same grid. Prefix-sum each family once and a whole diagonal run — here $5+9$ — is a difference of two stored numbers, no loop over the run.

:::

Because every cell falls on exactly one diagonal of each family, the buckets together hold just the $O(nm)$ original cells, and filling them takes a single pass. Diagonal sums show up in grid-path and "bishop-like" counting problems; the real lesson is that "prefix" means "cumulative along whatever 1D line you are slicing," not only along rows.

## A6. Weighted prefix sums & triage {#sec-nd-a6}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
The last shape is a **weighted** sum: instead of "what is in this range," you are asked to add up every element a known number of times, or scaled by a factor that depends on its position. Two tools cover most of it. First, **per-element multiplicity**: the sum of all contiguous sub-array totals equals $\sum_i a_i \cdot (i+1)(n-i)$, because element $i$ sits inside $(i+1)$ choices of left end and $(n-i)$ choices of right end — count how many times each cell is used, then one weighted pass. Second, **value-domain prefixing**: precompute a property for every candidate value and lay a prefix count along the value axis, so "how many $x\in[\ell,r]$ have $g(x)=k$" is one table lookup. Both are the prefix idea with a *weight* folded into the stored partial sum.
:::

The multiplicity identity in code, checked against the double-loop sum of every subarray:

```{python}
def sum_all_subarrays(a):
    """Sum of sum(a[l..r]) over all 0-indexed l<=r: each a[i] counted (i+1)*(n-i) times."""
    n = len(a)
    return sum(a[i] * (i + 1) * (n - i) for i in range(n))


def sum_all_subarrays_brute(a):
    n = len(a)
    s = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            s += sum(a[i:j + 1])
    return s


assert sum_all_subarrays([1, 2, 3]) == 20     # [1]+[2]+[3]+[1,2]+[2,3]+[1,2,3]
for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(-8, 8) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    assert sum_all_subarrays(a) == sum_all_subarrays_brute(a)
```

The multiplicity weight $(i+1)(n-i)$ grows like $n^2$, so with $a_i$ up to $10^{9}$ and $n$ up to $10^{5}$ the total can reach $\sim 10^{19}$ — past even $2^{63}$. This is the @sec-nd-pit overflow trap in its sharpest form: use 64-bit, and if the bound truly exceeds $9.2\times 10^{18}$, take the answer modulo a given number *inside* the accumulation.

Now the triage that closes the chapter. When you read a statement, ask two questions: **are the values fixed or changing, and is the slice an axis-aligned box or a custom shape?**

::: {#fig-nd-a6}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.flow(ax, p, {
        "root": (0.0, 2.6, "sum over ranges\nof a flat array/grid?", "muted"),
        "static": (-4.2, 0.2, "fixed values,\nmany reads", "green"),
        "updates": (0.0, 0.2, "many ADDS, read\nat the end", "indigo"),
        "dynamic": (4.2, 0.2, "interleaved\nupdate + query", "violet"),
        "pref": (-4.2, -2.4, "prefix table\n1D/2D/3D, diagonals\n(this ch.)", "green"),
        "diff": (0.0, -2.4, "difference array\n1st / 2nd order\n(this ch.)", "indigo"),
        "bit": (4.2, -2.4, "Fenwick / 2D BIT\n(online; @sec-ds)", "pink"),
    }, [("root", "static", ""), ("root", "updates", ""), ("root", "dynamic", ""),
        ("static", "pref", "O(1)/query"), ("updates", "diff", "O(1)/update"),
        ("dynamic", "bit", "O(log^d n)")], w=3.1, h=1.3)
V.show(draw)
```

The decision tree. Fixed values read many ways (line, box, diagonal, weighted) all want a **prefix** table; a batch of adds that you only read after wants a **difference** array; updates and queries *interleaved* online push you to a Fenwick/2D-BIT (@sec-ds), and a large offline batch whose answer needs a moving value-structure pushes to Mo (@sec-mo). Everything before that line is this chapter.

:::

- **Static, arbitrary-shape slice** (box, diagonal): precompute the right prefix table — A1, A3, A5.
- **Batched constant/linear updates, one final read**: the difference array, first-order (A2) or second-order (A4).
- **Count over a value domain**: precompute per value, then prefix along it — @sec-nd-p1-rq (CF 932B).
- **Every subarray / every pair, weighted**: multiplicity counting, one weighted pass — @sec-nd-p4-rybinsk (CF 1195D2).
- **Interleaved online updates**: not here — a Fenwick / 2D-BIT in @sec-ds.
- **Offline batch, hard-to-decompose answer**: reorder and slide a window, @sec-mo.

A caution for Part B: several famous "matrix" and "sum" problems are *not* prefix-sum problems. CF 718C "Sasha and Array" and CF 1252K "Addition Robot" carry a `matrices` tag but are solved by a segment tree with matrix exponentiation; CF 844B "Rectangles" is a probability expectation; CF 1648A "Weird Sum" is a separable-axis *contribution* count already solved in another chapter. They look at home in this family and are cited as practice, never as worked examples.


## Part B — Patterns

Part B turns the six lessons into four worked patterns. Each opens with the signal that calls it up and a template box, then solves two problems — a judge problem where one exists, and a self-authored task that isolates the move. Every solution is checked against a brute force and a random stress.

## P1. Prefix sums, one and two dimensions {#sec-nd-p1}

**Where we are.** The 1D prefix sum is the seed of the whole chapter: one table, $O(1)$ per range question. The first problem keeps the *shape* of a 1D array but moves the axis to the **value domain** — you prefix-sum over "which $x$ have this property" rather than over positions. The second lifts the table into a genuine grid.

**Recognise it.** A fixed data set, many "add up this range/box" questions, and $n\cdot m$ small enough to precompute once but the query count large enough that $O(\text{area})$ per query is too slow.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Build `P` once with `P[i+1][j+1] = P[i][j+1] + rowsum` (@sec-nd-a1); answer a half-open rectangle $[r_0,r_1)\times[c_0,c_1)$ with `rect_sum = P[r1][c1] - P[r0][c1] - P[r1][c0] + P[r0][c0]`. On a value domain, sort/bucket by the property and prefix the counts, then a range count is two table reads (@sec-nd-a6). Build $O(nm)$, query $O(1)$; keep the table in 64-bit.
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-932b-recursive-queries/problem.qmd >}}

[**From counting values on a line to summing a grid.** *Recursive Queries* prefixes along a single (value) axis and reads a range with one subtraction. Put the data on two axes and the identical move needs the four-corner inclusion–exclusion instead of two table reads — that is the sub-rectangle problem below.]{.flow-bridge}

### Problem: Static Sub-Rectangle Sums {#sec-nd-p1-rectsum}

::: {.p-statement}
A grid of $n$ rows and $m$ columns of integers ($1 \le n, m \le 10^{3}$, $|a_{ij}| \le 10^{9}$) is given once, then $q$ questions ($1 \le q \le 2\cdot 10^{5}$). Each question names two opposite corners of an axis-aligned sub-rectangle and asks for the sum of the cells inside it. Answer every question.

Source: *self-authored* — designed to exercise @sec-nd-a1 in isolation; validated against an $O(\text{area})$ brute force and a random stress (no judge link).

Example — on $[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]$ the whole grid sums to $45$, the bottom-right $2\times2$ to $28$, and the top row to $6$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Everything is fixed, so pay one $O(nm)$ cost up front to build the 2D prefix table $P$, then every rectangle is the four-corner inclusion–exclusion of @sec-nd-a1 — $O(1)$, independent of how big the rectangle is. A million-area query costs the same as a single cell.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Per query, walk the cells.** Sum the rectangle directly. $O(q\cdot nm)$ up to $2\cdot 10^{11}$ — reference only.
2. **Prefix once, query in four reads.** Build `P = build_prefix2d(a)`, answer each question with `rect_sum`. $O(nm + q)$.

**Invariant.** `rect_sum(P, r0, c0, r1, c1)` equals $\sum_{r_0 \le r < r_1 \atop c_0 \le c < c_1} a[r][c]$ by the inclusion–exclusion proved in @sec-nd-a1.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Sum the cells of each rectangle

::: {.form-next}
Loop over the rectangle for every query. $O(\text{area})$ per question; the oracle.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def rectsum_brute(a, queries):
    return [sum(a[i][j] for i in range(r0, r1) for j in range(c0, c1))
            for (r0, c0, r1, c1) in queries]


assert rectsum_brute([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]],
                     [(0, 0, 3, 3), (1, 1, 3, 3), (0, 0, 1, 3)]) == [45, 28, 6]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// brute force: for each query sum the cells of [r0,r1) x [c0,c1) (fragment, needs <bits/stdc++.h>)
long long rectsum_brute(const vector<vector<long long> >& a,
                        const vector<array<int, 4> >& qs) {
    long long total = 0;
    for (size_t qi = 0; qi < qs.size(); ++qi) {
        int r0 = qs[qi][0], c0 = qs[qi][1], r1 = qs[qi][2], c1 = qs[qi][3];
        for (int i = r0; i < r1; ++i)
            for (int j = c0; j < c1; ++j)
                total += a[i][j];
    }
    return total;
}
```
:::

#### Build the 2D prefix table once

::: {.form-next}
One $O(nm)$ build, then each query is four table reads. Reuses `build_prefix2d` / `rect_sum` from @sec-nd-a1.
:::

    _P = build_prefix2d(_a)
    V.grid(ax, p, [[str(_P[i][j]) for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)], x=0.0, y=0.0,
           row_labels=["P0", "P1", "P2", "P3"], col_labels=["0", "1", "2", "3"],
           colors={(2, 2): "green", (0, 2): "pink", (2, 0): "pink", (0, 0): "indigo"})
